text: A famine struck during David's reign for three straight years, so David sought the LORD's guidance, and the LORD answered that Saul and his household bore bloodguilt for putting the Gibeonites to death.

The king summoned the Gibeonites to speak with them — they were not actually Israelites but a remnant of the Amorites whom Israel had sworn an oath to spare, though Saul, out of misplaced zeal for Israel and Judah, had tried to wipe them out.
David asked them what he could do for them, and how he could make things right so they would bless the LORD's people again.
The Gibeonites told him it wasn't a matter of silver or gold between them and Saul's house, nor did they want any random Israelite put to death; David asked again what they wanted done.
They answered that the man who destroyed them and schemed to wipe them out so they'd have no place left anywhere in Israel's territory —
they wanted seven of his male descendants handed over, to be executed before the LORD at Gibeah, Saul's own town, and the king agreed to give them.
But the king spared Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson, because of the oath David and Jonathan had sworn to each other before the LORD.

Instead David took the two sons Rizpah daughter of Aiah had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, along with the five sons Saul's daughter Merab had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite,
and handed them over to the Gibeonites, who executed them on the mountain before the LORD; all seven died together at the very start of the barley harvest.

Rizpah daughter of Aiah spread sackcloth for herself on the rock and kept watch there from the start of harvest until rain finally fell from the sky, keeping the birds away by day and wild animals away by night.
Word of what Rizpah, Saul's concubine, had done reached David.

So David went and retrieved the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the leaders of Jabesh-gilead, who had secretly taken them from the public square at Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them up the day they killed Saul at Gilboa.
He brought back the bones of Saul and Jonathan from there, and they also gathered up the bones of the men who had just been executed.
They buried Saul and Jonathan's bones in Benjamin's territory at Zela, in Kish's family tomb, carrying out everything the king had ordered — and after that, God answered the prayers for the land.
War broke out again between the Philistines and Israel, and David went out to fight alongside his men, but he grew exhausted.
Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of the giants, whose bronze spear weighed three hundred shekels and who carried a new sword, intended to kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his rescue, struck the Philistine down, and killed him; after that David's men made him swear he would never go out to battle with them again, so the lamp of Israel wouldn't be snuffed out.
Later there was more fighting with the Philistines at Gob, where Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, another descendant of the giants.

There was still more fighting with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim, from Bethlehem, killed the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was as thick as a weaver's beam.
Then there was fighting at Gath, where there was a huge man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all, also descended from the giants.
When he taunted Israel, Jonathan, son of David's brother Shimeah, struck him down.
These four were all descendants of the giants at Gath, and all of them fell at the hands of David and his men.
